attacks.claim: The cost math treats the daily token volume as monthly. 38M lines/day x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens/day, which is ~$1,140 per day at $0.50/1M, or ~$34k/month, plus ~$200/month output. That is roughly 23x the $1,500/month approved budget, and peak days (61M lines) cost ~$1,830 in input alone. There is no per-day spend cap or budget alert.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: All application logs after redaction are sent to a third-party LLM. Redaction covers only four categories, so names, customer identifiers, and free-text user content in exception messages will reach the vendor without any coverage analysis of what the logs actually contain.
attacks.evidence: "already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)"

attacks.claim: Each 5-minute per-service call carries roughly 264k input tokens on average (about 4,400 lines x 60 tokens), more at peak. The plan does not confirm that Corvid-mini's context window fits this, nor how truncation or sampling would work. It also does not address provider rate limits (tokens per minute), which peak incident load would hit hardest.
attacks.evidence: "sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt" and "Model: Corvid-mini, $0.50 per 1M input tokens"

attacks.claim: log-tap is added to the shared Vector production pipeline with no backpressure or drop policy. If the Redis queue or the LLM slows, the pipeline could stall or silently lose logs for production services, and the plan does not say which.
attacks.evidence: "log-tap (new): subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage and forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue."

attacks.claim: Summaries are generated on a 5-minute cadence, so the attached summary can be several minutes stale and does not match the goal of 'within seconds of a page'. Nothing marks staleness, and a failed or stopped summarizer would leave old summaries attached to the incident with no signal to responders.
attacks.evidence: "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service" and "The PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries"

attacks.claim: Untrusted log content (user-supplied strings echoed into logs) goes straight into the LLM prompt, and the model output is posted into PagerDuty incident comments. A crafted log line could steer the summary, including the 'suspected deploy' field, and there is no prompt-injection or output-validation step.
attacks.evidence: "stores a structured summary (top errors, new error signatures, affected endpoints, suspected deploy)" and "auto-comment with the latest summaries for the paging service"

attacks.claim: The staffing estimate assumes both engineers spend 100% of six weeks on the build, but the charter says on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time. Real capacity is roughly 6 eng-weeks, not 12, so the schedule would roughly double.
attacks.evidence: "Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)." versus "on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time"

attacks.claim: The business case rests on unmeasured premises: that the first 15-20 minutes are spent grepping, and that summaries will cut median MTTR from 47 to 30 minutes. The launch gate only measures summary quality on 40 replayed incidents and never tests whether MTTR moves.
attacks.evidence: "instead of spending the first 15-20 minutes grepping logs across 30 services" and "Launch gate: >= 70% useful, <= 5% misleading."

attacks.claim: No kill switch or disable path is described for the log-tap or the PagerDuty auto-comments. If the feature misbehaves mid-incident, the only stated safeguard is the claim that summaries are advisory.
attacks.evidence: "Summaries are advisory only. Alert rules, paging, and escalation policies are unchanged."

attacks.claim: The 'suspected deploy' field has no stated derivation method, and the gate tolerates up to 5% misleading summaries. A wrong deploy suggestion could steer responders toward an unnecessary rollback.
All production logs depend on a single LLM vendor with no fallback model, no stated data residency, and no exit plan. An outage or price change would disable the feature with no alternative.
Zero retention is asserted but not verified, and the plan does not say whether customer data in logs is covered by the vendor's DPA or by subprocessor notice obligations to customers.
attacks.evidence: "Corvid account has zero-retention enabled; data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)."

attacks.claim: The prompt is described as fixed, but there is no versioning or regression process for prompt or model changes, so eval results from the 40-incident replay cannot be tied to the production behaviour later.
